sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Shàngdì** ​(*shangdi*) — ‌Supreme ‌Deity, Heaven, ​Sovereign · ​Highest ​Emperor; the ​supreme ​god of ‌early ​Chinese religion ​— belongs ‌to ​the Chinese ‌tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ​the domain ​"Supreme ​Deity, Heaven, ​Sovereign". ‌The name ​means ‌"Highest Emperor; ​the ‌supreme god ​of early ‌Chinese ​religion"[^1].

**Shàngdì** ‌belongs ​to the ​Chinese ‌tradition, where ‌it is ‌associated ​with supreme ​deity, ‌heaven, sovereign.[^2]

​PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name as ​**Shàngdì** ​and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[shangdi.com](https://punicodex.com/shangdi/). ​The restoration ​preserves at ​least ​one distinctive ‌feature ‌— a ​diacritic ‌or a ​distinctive letter ​— ‌that the ‌ASCII ‌form loses, ‌and ​exactly one ‌historically valid ​Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which ‌places the ​name ​in Tier ​1. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ​*shangdi* ​survives as ‌a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ​system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^2].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Chinese ‌characters as ​**上帝**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Highest Emperor; ​the supreme ​god of ‌early Chinese ​religion"[^1].

Shàng ​(上) 'above, ‌highest'; Dì ​(帝) 'emperor, ‌thearch' — ​the high ‌god of ​Shang and ​Zhou religion, ​later identified ​with Tian.

​The ASCII ‌form *shangdi* ​survives only ‌because the ​early domain-name ‌system could ​not carry ‌diacritics; it ​is a ‌technological compromise, ​not an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ‌restoration **Shàngdì** ‌recovers the ​stress accent ​of the ‌original directly ​in the ​address bar. ‌The restoration ​preserves at ​least one ‌distinctive feature — ​a diacritic ‌or a ​distinctive letter ​— that ​the ASCII ​form loses, ‌and exactly ‌one historically ​valid Unicode ‌restoration exists, ​which places ​the name ‌in Tier ‌1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**s** → ‌**S** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **h** ​→ **h** ‌— Same
​- **a** ​→ **à** ​— Grave ‌tone mark
​- **n** ​→ **n** ​— Same
‌- **g** ​→ **g** ‌— Same
​- **d** ‌→ **d** ​— Same
‌- **i** ‌→ **ì** ​— Grave ​tone mark

​The canonical ​temple for ‌this name ‌is served ​at **shangdi.com**[^2].

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name is ​**/shangdi/** ​— ​Chinese ‌Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

​- ‌**S** ​— Initial ‌character ​of ​the ​restored ​form ​Shàngdì.
‌- ​**hàngdì** ‌— Remainder ​of ‌the ​name, ‌preserving ​the ‌distinctive ​marks ​of ‌the ‌Chinese tradition.

‌For ​the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: ​'SHANGDI' ‌— pronounce ​the ‌restored ​form ​with ​attention ​to ‌the ‌preserved ​diacritics ‌and length.

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the ​name:

‌- ​**Chinese** ​— Shàngdì, ​the ‌restored ​Unicode ​form ​of ‌the ​name

​Shàngdì ​is Tier ‌1 ​because ‌the ​Chinese ‌form ​preserves ‌distinctive ‌features ​that ​ASCII loses: ​stress, ​length, ‌or ‌special ​characters.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌**Shàngdì** ‌circulate within ​the Chinese ​corpus, ​where the ​figure ​embodies supreme ‌deity, ​heaven, sovereign.[^1]

​### Primary ‌Attestation ​(Sources)

Shàngdì ‌is ​attested in ‌the ​canonical Chinese ​sources as ​a ​figure associated ​with ‌supreme deity, ​heaven, ‌sovereign.[^1]

### ​Name ‌and Meaning ​(Etymology)

The ‌name ​means "Highest ‌Emperor; ​the supreme ​god ‌of early ‌Chinese religion" ‌and ​reflects the ​figure's ‌role in ​the ​tradition. **Shàngdì**, ‌the Supreme ​Lord, ​was the ‌high ​god of ‌the ​Shang and ​early Zhou ​dynasties. ​He received ‌sacrifices ‌from the ​Son ‌of Heaven ​and controlled ​harvest, ‌warfare, and ‌the ‌weather.[^1] Later ‌Chinese ​religion absorbed ‌Shàngdì into ​the ​more bureaucratic ​Tiāndào, ‌but the ​name ​retained its ​aura ‌of absolute, ​personal sovereignty. ​Oracle ​bones ask ‌whether ​Shàngdì will ‌grant ​rain, bless ‌the harvest, ​or ‌approve a ‌military ​campaign, revealing ​a ​direct, petitionary ​relationship between ‌king ‌and high ​god.[^1]
